query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Pulsed electric current‐assisted annealing (ECA) applied to as‐cast eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 will promote controlled, electromigration‐driven solute segregation at the semi‐coherent lamellar phase boundaries and modestly refine the lamellar spacing. This tailored interfacial chemistry will strengthen the boundaries and delay microcrack nucleation, thus simultaneously enhancing room‐temperature tensile yield strength and ductility relative to the unmodified lamellar baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high‐entropy alloy exhibiting a dual‐phase lamellar (fcc/B2) microstructure with relatively coarse lamellae and conventional interfacial chemistry.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to pulsed electric current-assisted annealing at a moderate temperature (e.g., ~600 °C) for a short duration (e.g., 5–10 minutes) under controlled current density.
generation.conditions: The treatment must be carried out under conditions that drive modest electromigration without causing unwanted bulk phase transformations or excessive grain growth; the current pulses should be optimized to enhance localized diffusion specifically at the lamellar interfaces.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced selective segregation of solute atoms (e.g., Cr and possibly other species present) to the semi-coherent fcc/B2 phase boundaries, along with slight refinement of the lamellar spacing.
generation.mechanism: The pulsed electric current accelerates atom mobility via electromigration, concentrating specific elements at the phase boundaries to form ultra-thin, chemically modified interfacial layers that increase interfacial cohesion. This improved bonding at boundaries mitigates stress concentrations and delays microcrack initiation. In parallel, slight refinement in lamellar spacing leads to enhanced back‐stress hardening during deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified as‐cast (or conventionally annealed) lamellar structure, the ECA-treated alloy will exhibit a measurable increase in yield strength (e.g., on the order of 10–15% higher) and a significant improvement in tensile ductility (e.g., 20–30% increase in elongation) at room temperature.
generation.baseline: Eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 processed by conventional annealing without the application of pulsed electric current, displaying typical lamellar architectures with unmodified interfacial chemistry.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected only when the current density and annealing time are carefully optimized; excessive current or prolonged treatment could lead to coarsening, undesired phase changes, or degradation of mechanical properties. The intervention is applicable primarily to alloys with eutectic lamellar microstructures containing semi‐coherent phase boundaries.
generation.uncertainty: While previous studies (e.g., PMC6175879 and PMC6687781) have demonstrated the importance of interfacial chemistry and heterogeneity for strength–ductility synergy, the use of pulsed electric current to deliberately modify interface composition in EHEAs is untested. The exact segregation profiles and resulting mechanical effects under these conditions are uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 samples: one set processed with pulsed electric current-assisted annealing (using optimized parameters) and a control set processed under identical thermal conditions without current. Use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and atom probe tomography (APT) to characterize lamellar spacing and interfacial segregation. Then conduct room-temperature tensile tests and in situ micro-mechanical (e.g., micro-cantilever bending) tests to evaluate microcrack initiation and propagation.
measurements: Tensile yield strength and elongation to failure (ductility)
Lamellar spacing and interface chemistry (via TEM and APT)
Onset and propagation characteristics of microcracks during in situ testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ECA-treated samples do not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in both yield strength and ductility (relative to controls) and if microstructural analysis fails to reveal the predicted enhanced interfacial segregation and lamellar refinement, then the hypothesis is falsified.
